{{Short description|Relation on disjoint pairs of sets}}
{{No footnotes|date=September 2008}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''separoid''' is a [[binary relation]] between [[disjoint sets]] which is stable as an [[ideal (order theory)|ideal]] in the canonical order induced by [[subset|inclusion]]. Many mathematical objects which appear to be quite different, find a common generalisation in the framework of separoids; e.g., [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]], configurations of [[convex set]]s, [[oriented matroid]]s, and [[polytopes]]. Any countable [[Category (mathematics)|category]] is an induced subcategory of separoids when they are endowed with [[homomorphism]]s<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Strausz | first1=Ricardo
| title=Homomorphisms of separoids
| journal=Electronic Notes in Discrete Mathematics
| volume=28
| date=1 March 2007
| pages=461–468
| doi=10.1016/j.endm.2007.01.064
| zbl=1291.05036}}</ref> (viz., mappings that preserve the so-called ''[[Radon's theorem|minimal Radon partitions]]'').

In this general framework, some results and invariants of different categories turn out to be special cases of the same aspect; e.g., the pseudoachromatic number from graph theory and the [[Tverberg theorem]] from combinatorial convexity are simply two faces of the same aspect, namely, complete colouring of separoids.

== The axioms ==

A '''separoid'''<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Strausz | first1=Ricardo
| title=Separoids and a Tverberg-type problem
| journal=[[Geombinatorics]]
| volume=15
| year=2005
| issue=2
| pages=79–92
| zbl=1090.52005}}</ref> is a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>S</math> endowed with a binary relation <math>\mid\ \subseteq2^S\times2^S</math> on its [[power set]], which satisfies the following simple properties for <math>A,B\subseteq S</math>:

: <math>A\mid B\Leftrightarrow B\mid A,</math>
: <math>A\mid B\Rightarrow A\cap B=\varnothing,</math>
: <math>A\mid B \hbox{ and } A'\subset A\Rightarrow A'\mid B.</math>

A related pair <math>A\mid B</math> is called a '''separation''' and we often say that ''A is separated from B''. It is enough to know the ''maximal'' separations to reconstruct the separoid.

A [[Map (mathematics)|mapping]] <math>\varphi\colon S\to T</math> is a [[morphism]] of separoids if the preimages of separations are separations; that is, for <math>A,B\subseteq T</math>

: <math>A\mid B\Rightarrow\varphi^{-1}(A)\mid\varphi^{-1}(B).</math>

== Examples ==

Examples of separoids can be found in almost every branch of [[mathematics]].<ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Arocha | first1=Jorge Luis
| last2=Bracho | first2=Javier
| last3=Montejano | first3=Luis
| last4=Oliveros | first4=Deborah | author4-link = Déborah Oliveros
| last5=Strausz | first5=Ricardo
| title=Separoids, their categories and a Hadwiger-type theorem for transversals
| journal=[[Discrete and Computational Geometry]]
| volume=27
| year=2002
| issue=3
| pages=377–385
| doi=10.1007/s00454-001-0075-2 | doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
| last1=Nešetřil | first1=Jaroslav | authorlink1=Jaroslav Nešetřil
| last2=Strausz | first2=Ricardo
| title=Universality of separoids
| journal=Archivum Mathematicum (Brno)
| volume=42
| year=2006
| issue=1
| pages=85–101
| url=https://www.emis.de/journals/AM/06-1/neset1.pdf}}</ref><ref name="M-BS">{{cite journal
| last1=Montellano-Ballesteros | first1=Juan José
| last2=Strausz | first2=Ricardo
| title=A characterization of cocircuit graphs of uniform oriented matroids
| journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
| series=Series B
| volume=96
| issue=4
| date=July 2006
| pages=445–454
| doi=10.1016/j.jctb.2005.09.008 | doi-access=free
| zbl=1109.52016}}</ref> Here we list just a few.

1. Given a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] G=(V,E), we can define a separoid on its [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] by saying that two (disjoint) subsets of V, say A and B, are separated if there are no [[Edge (graph theory)|edges]] going from one to the other; i.e.,

: <math>A\mid B\Leftrightarrow\forall a\in A\hbox{ and }b\in B\colon ab\not\in E.</math>

2. Given an oriented matroid<ref name="M-BS"/> ''M'' = (''E'',''T''), given in terms of its topes ''T'', we can define a separoid on ''E'' by saying that two subsets are separated if they are contained in opposite signs of a tope. In other words, the topes of an oriented matroid are the ''maximal'' separations of a separoid. This example includes, of course, all [[directed graph]]s.

3. Given a family of objects in a [[Euclidean space]], we can define a separoid in it by saying that two subsets are separated if there exists a [[hyperplane]] that ''separates'' them; i.e., leaving them in the two opposite sides of it.

4. Given a [[topological space]], we can define a separoid saying that two subsets are separated if there exist two disjoint [[open set]]s which contains them (one for each of them).

== The basic lemma ==

Every separoid can be represented with a family of convex sets in some Euclidean space and their separations by hyperplanes.
